# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The rapid expansion of transcatheter therapies for structural heart disease has created a parallel demand for reliable large-bore vascular access. Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) and emerging transcatheter mitral and aortic interventions increasingly require delivery systems of 14–22 French [1]. While transfemoral access remains the default route, a substantial minority of patients have iliofemoral disease that precludes safe sheath insertion [2]. Transcaval access—deliberate crossing from the inferior vena cava (IVC) into the abdominal aorta—has emerged as a percutaneous alternative to surgical and transapical approaches [3].

## Concept and Rationale

Transcaval access exploits the anatomic proximity of the IVC and abdominal aorta within the retroperitoneum [4]. An electrified guidewire is advanced from the caval lumen into the aorta, creating a controlled aortocaval fistula through which a large-bore sheath is delivered [5]. The retroperitoneal tissue and elevated intra-aortic pressure relative to caval pressure promote spontaneous tract closure, and the tract can be sealed with a nitinol occluder device [6]. The technique was pioneered in preclinical models before its first-in-human application by Greenbaum and colleagues [7].

## Procedural Technique

The procedure begins with computed tomographic angiography to identify a target aortic crossing zone free of calcification, ideally below the renal arteries and above the aortic bifurcation [8]. A snare or marker catheter is positioned in the aorta to serve as a fluoroscopic target and to capture the crossing wire [9]. Electrosurgical energy applied to a back-end of a stiff guidewire enables atraumatic traversal of the aortic wall, after which the wire is snared and externalized to establish a rail [10]. The large-bore sheath is then advanced across the tract for valve delivery [11]. Upon completion, the tract is closed using a nitinol duct occluder, with completion aortography confirming hemostasis [12].

## Clinical Evidence

The prospective multicenter Transcaval Access Study demonstrated procedural success in the large majority of patients with prohibitive peripheral access, validating feasibility for TAVR [13]. Subsequent registries reported transcaval access success rates exceeding 95%, with valve implantation accomplished in nearly all cases [14]. Comparative analyses have suggested that transcaval TAVR yields outcomes comparable to other alternative access routes such as transaxillary and transcarotid approaches [15]. Single-center series have confirmed reproducibility and acceptable safety with growing operator experience [16].

The most feared complications relate to retroperitoneal bleeding from the aortotomy [17]. Reported life-threatening or major bleeding occurs in a meaningful minority of cases, although many bleeds are managed percutaneously with covered stents or repeat occluder deployment [18]. Importantly, residual aortocaval fistulae are frequently observed on follow-up imaging but are usually small, hemodynamically insignificant, and often close spontaneously over time [19]. Long-term follow-up has not demonstrated adverse cardiac remodeling attributable to persistent shunting in most patients [20].

## Comparison with Alternative Access

For patients ineligible for transfemoral access, transcaval competes with transapical, transaortic, transaxillary/subclavian, and transcarotid routes [21]. Transapical and transaortic access require surgical exposure and have been associated with higher morbidity and slower recovery [22]. Transcaval offers a fully percutaneous alternative that avoids thoracotomy, a particular advantage in frail patients with respiratory compromise [23]. Registry comparisons indicate that transcaval mortality and stroke rates are broadly similar to transcarotid and transaxillary approaches, although bleeding profiles differ [24]. The choice of access ultimately depends on individual anatomy, operator expertise, and institutional protocols [25].

## Patient Selection and Imaging

Meticulous CT planning is the cornerstone of safe transcaval access [26]. Operators assess the IVC–aorta relationship, identify a calcium-free aortic target, and exclude interposed structures such as bowel or large lumbar veins [27]. Adequate apposition of the IVC and aorta, with minimal intervening retroperitoneal fat, predicts favorable outcomes [28]. Anatomic exclusion criteria include heavy circumferential aortic calcification and aortic aneurysm or graft at the crossing site [29].

## Future Directions and Conclusion

Transcaval access has matured from an investigational maneuver into an established option within the structural heart toolkit. Dedicated closure devices and refined crossing technologies promise to reduce bleeding complications further, and the technique may broaden to support emerging large-bore mitral and mechanical circulatory support systems [30]. With careful imaging-based patient selection and increasing operator familiarity, transcaval access provides a valuable, fully percutaneous solution for patients otherwise denied transcatheter therapy. Ongoing prospective data collection will refine its role relative to other alternative access strategies.
